title: Mars: A Planet That Lost Its Water
objective: After this level you can describe the evidence that Mars once had liquid water.
summary: Dry riverbeds and ancient lakes show Mars was once wetter. Rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance are reading that history.

cards.headline: Mars has riverbeds. It just doesn’t have rivers anymore.
cards.body: Dried river valleys and old lake beds are carved into Mars. So where did the water go, and how do we know it was ever there?

cards.headline: A thin, dry world
cards.body: Start with the air. Mars's atmosphere is thin and mostly carbon dioxide, with less than 1% of Earth's surface air pressure. Venus has far too much air; Mars has barely any. And the water? Most of what Mars has today is frozen, in its polar ice caps and underground. The rivers are gone. The water is in the freezer.

cards.headline: Clues of a wetter past
cards.body: Mars kept the receipts. Dry river valleys and ancient lake beds show that liquid water once flowed there. Then we sent a robot to check in person. NASA's Curiosity rover, which landed in 2012, found that Gale Crater once held a lake. Picture a crater as dry as a parking lot that used to be a place you could have gone for a swim.
cards.callout: Curiosity, 2012: Gale Crater once held a lake

cards.fact: Perseverance landed in 2021 in an ancient lake and river delta.
cards.context: Curiosity showed that Mars once had lakes. NASA's Perseverance rover went straight to one: Jezero Crater, the site of an old lake and river delta. It's collecting rock samples there. If you want to know what an old lake left behind, you go and pick up its stones.

cards.headline: Mars: investigated
learned: Mars’s air is thin: under 1% of Earth’s pressure
Riverbeds and lake beds show a wetter past
Curiosity (2012) found an ancient lake in Gale Crater

questions.prompt: Where is most of Mars’s water today?

options.label: In deep oceans beneath the red dust
options.rationale: Its water is frozen, not in oceans.

options.label: In rivers that flow during the summer
options.rationale: Liquid water can’t last on the surface.

options.label: Frozen in polar ice caps and underground
In thick clouds that cover the planet
options.rationale: Mars’s thin air holds little water.

questions.explanation: Mars’s thin atmosphere can’t keep water liquid, so most of it is frozen in polar caps and underground.

questions.prompt: What did the Curiosity rover discover at Gale Crater?

options.label: That the crater once held a lake
That the crater is an active volcano
options.rationale: That’s Olympus Mons, elsewhere on Mars.

options.label: That the crater is full of liquid water
options.rationale: Its lake dried up long ago.

options.label: That the crater was made by Phobos
options.rationale: Its discovery was about water, not its origin.

questions.explanation: Curiosity found evidence that Gale Crater once held a lake, part of the case for a wetter ancient Mars.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: Mars is the outermost rocky planet. How does its air compare with Earth’s?

options.label: Much thicker, like Venus’s
options.rationale: Venus has the crushing air; Mars’s is thin.

questions.explanation: Mars’s atmosphere is thin and mostly carbon dioxide, with less than 1% of Earth’s surface air pressure.
